content: 1. Large containers must be opened and stirred thoroughly multiple times to ensure proper mixing. After this process, the container should not have a sticky layer of undispersed material at the bottom. 2. To check for the presence of a sticky, undispersed layer (referred to as cake), a glass rod or a similar device, appropriately sized for the container, can be used to probe the bottom. 3. All physical and chemical tests must be conducted on a sample taken after the recommended homogenization procedure has been performed. 4. Analytical methods used must comply with CIPAC, AOAC, or equivalent standards. If the methods are unpublished, full details and appropriate validation data must be submitted to FAO/WHO by the proposer. 5. Homogenization must be performed carefully to avoid aeration of the sample, which can lead to errors in determining mass per milliliter and active ingredient content (in g/L), especially if methods other than OECD 109 are used. 6. If both g/kg and g/L at 20°C are required by the buyer, in case of dispute, the analytical results should be calculated as g/kg. 7. Only relevant impurities should be included in the specification, and the title should reflect the name of the relevant impurity. Analytical methods must be peer-validated. 8. The method to be used for analysis must be explicitly stated. If multiple methods are available, a referee method must be selected. 9. Chemical assay is the most reliable method to measure the mass of active ingredients still in suspension. However, simpler methods like gravimetric or solvent-extraction determination may be used routinely, provided they yield results equivalent to the chemical assay method. In case of dispute, the chemical method will serve as the referee method. 10. The mass of the sample used in testing should correspond to the highest recommended rate of use by the supplier, provided it falls within the scope of the method. Testing should be conducted in CIPAC standard water D. 11. Percentages may be specified in one or more ranges, as appropriate for the product. 12. Laser diffraction is not always suitable for measuring the particle size distribution of liquid formulations. 13. Samples of the formulation taken before and after the storage stability test should be analyzed concurrently after the test to minimize analytical error. 14. Aqueous capsule suspensions (CS) are stable suspensions of micro-encapsulated active ingredients in an aqueous continuous phase, intended for dilution with water before use. 15. Parameters describing CS performance include active ingredient determination (total, free, and release rate), pourability, spontaneity of dispersion, suspensibility, wet sieve and persistent foam tests, and stability to freezing/thawing. 16. Freezing of micro-encapsulated formulations may cause capsule failure due to crystallization or other mechanisms, leading to significant changes in formulation properties, including the release of active ingredients into the aqueous medium. 17. Oil dispersions (OD) are stable suspensions of active ingredients in an organic fluid, intended for dilution with water before use. They are metastable systems and may require re-homogenization after transport or storage. 18. OD formulations do not disperse as spontaneously as emulsifiable concentrates (EC) upon dilution in water, necessitating stirring to achieve a homogeneous dispersion before application. 19. Parameters describing OD performance include pourability, dispersion stability, wet sieve and persistent foam tests, and storage stability at elevated temperatures to ensure the absence of crystal growth. 20. Suspo-emulsions (SE) are mixtures of water-insoluble active ingredients dispersed in an aqueous solution, with some active ingredients in suspension form and others in emulsion form. They are intended for dilution in water before spray application. 21. SE formulations are not indefinitely stable, and their suitability for use after transport and storage must be ensured through testing of parameters such as active ingredient identity and content, impurities, pourability, and dispersion stability. 22. SE formulations are easy to handle, measure, and mix with water, and they are dust-free, non-flammable, and compatible with water. However, they require stability testing under high and low-temperature conditions to ensure performance.
